summary: Charlotte-Genesee light at the Genesee River mouth, Rochester: tower lit 1822, pier lights kept by the same keepers until 1947, and a museum today.

lens.where: replica fourth-order lens in the restored lantern room, activated 1 Nov 2014 (LighthouseFriends)

structures.note: Forty feet (LighthouseFriends); the record gives 12.0 m; the USLHS table gives 30 ft

D9 tower on the west pier; the working pier light (LighthouseFriends)

access.note: Museum; tower and keeper's house tours Fridays to Sundays, 1 to 5 pm, 1 May to 1 Nov 2026 (society site).

events.note: Mehitabel Hincher paid $400 for a four-acre plot for lighthouse purposes (LighthouseFriends)
Forty-foot native sandstone tower; contract by Ashbel Symons; completed in seven months at $3,301
First lit in 1822
Two 2,600-foot piers built at the river mouth (LighthouseFriends)
Treasury report by Lieutenant Charles T. Platt finds the station in poor condition; proposed new stone light not built (LighthouseFriends)
Fourth-order Fresnel lens replaces the lamps and reflectors
Brick keeper's dwelling built beside the tower
Cast-iron tower established on the west pier, 5 Nov 1880
Charlotte-Genesee Lighthouse discontinued, 21 Feb 1881
Lantern room and fourth-order lens moved to a wooden beacon on the west pier; in operation 1 April 1884
Congress appropriates $4,300 for a steam fog signal in place of the bell (3 March 1891)
Six-inch steam whistle completed and ready 30 September 1893, on the old crib on the west pier
Pierhead beacon moved nearly 500 feet; fog signal building moved about 1,000 feet
Beacon at outer end of east pier established 25 May 1902; rear light on west pier discontinued
West pier light changed from fixed red to occulting white; generators and batteries installed
Charlotte Harbor, N.Y., changed to electric incandescent, two lights (Commissioner report)
Skeletal steel tower with red box replaces the west pier light and fog-signal structure
Pier light automated; last keeper Wilbur L. Folwell Sr. transferred
Assistant keeper Cuyler Cook drowned on 18 Aug 1853 after his boat capsized en route to the pier light; Samuel Phillips stranded at the beacon, rescued by lifeboat next day (LighthouseFriends)
Tower restored with replica lantern room; relit 18 June 1984 with a fourth-order lens from the Ninth Coast Guard District
Deeded to Monroe County, which leases the property to the historical society
D9 cylindrical tower installed on the west pier
Lantern room returned 25 Sept 2014; replica fourth-order lens activated 1 Nov 2014

corrections.proposed: Relit 1984 after restoration; replica lens activated 2014
corrections.why: The tower was first lit in 1822 (the record itself has 1822 first_lit); 1984 was the relighting after restoration and 2014 was the replica lens activation (LighthouseFriends).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record says active and gives a 2014 first light. The U.S. Lighthouse Society record says not an active aid to navigation and discontinued 1881, and LighthouseFriends says the working light is the 1995 D9 pier tower. The story follows the Society record for the old tower and LighthouseFriends for the working light.
LighthouseFriends and the Society record both give 1881 for the discontinuance. The 1884 beacon carried the same lantern and lens to a new support on the west pier; it is not a new light.

notes_for_editor: Sources read: LighthouseFriends (cite 1; secondary); U.S. Lighthouse Society place record 'Charlotte Genesee (Port of Genesee)' with 48 roster lines (cite 2). roster.py first matched the station to 'Charlotte Genesee Range Rear' (a minor aid with no roster); the port place was passed with --place charlotte-genesee-port-genesee. Light-House Board annual reports: volume 1891-1892, scan p. 186 (cite 3); volume labelled 1893 (report for the fiscal year ended 30 June 1894), scan pp. 500 and 511 (cite 4); volume 1895 (fiscal year ended 30 June 1895), scan p. 364 (cite 5); volume labelled 1896, scan p. 155 (cite 6). Commissioner of Lighthouses bound volume 1915-1922: the fiscal 1918 list at scan p. 345 (printed p. 31) (cite 7); the detailed estimate at scan p. 690 (printed p. 85), which repeats at scan p. 582 (printed p. 84) (cite 8). The estimate's year is not clear from the page. The society home page gives the 2026 hours (cite 9). Putnam's 1917 history (general) is no longer cited; it gives the 1822 date, which LighthouseFriends and the Society record also support, and the guide keeps general histories to general context. Not checked: NRHP 74001259 (the nomination is not digitised; the PDF is the 76-character placeholder); the 1822 contract and the 1853 drowning in newspapers (two earlier Chronicling America searches for Cook, Phillips and Genesee in 1853 found nothing); the Platt 1838 report in Treasury records; the 1884 relocation and the 1885 move of the iron tower (Light-House Board volumes before 1891 are not in the corpus). Disagreements left in the story: the tower height (LighthouseFriends 40 ft, used; the record 12.0 m; the USLHS table 30 ft); the focal height (USLHS table 83 ft or 25.3 m; the record 14.0 m; not used); the 1853 drowning rests on LighthouseFriends alone; the Stephenson death ('suspicions of foul play') appears only in LighthouseFriends, which gives no detail, and the story reports it as LighthouseFriends' statement. OCR: the 1893 volume has a passage on a schooner, the Collier, damaging the west pier walk, which gives July 1892 in one copy and July 1893 in another; it is left out because the year is unclear. The 1918 list's 'in-candescent' is a line-break hyphen; the checker normalises it. Fiscal-year labels: the fog-signal hours come from reports for the years ended 30 June 1894 and 30 June 1895; the 1918 list is for July 1917 to June 1918. The keeper roster's person slugs match roster.py output. Keepers' roster names are the archive's; the Coast Guard and post-1947 names are not used in the story.
